I have added a local version of cartridge for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade with color utilities by Ryland Dagger to BallyAlley.com.  It contains "Color Viewer, Color Matcher, and Color Table."

These three utilities for the Bally Astrocade run on a cartridge that help developers preview, compare, and select colors on real hardware. These tools make it easier to design palettes for games and demos while seeing exactly how colors appear on an actual console rather than an emulator.

The program can be downloaded on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/ml_tools.html#ColorsRylandDagger

Ryland updated this cartridge in late 2025.  It has been previously discussed in this thread:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/108109266

Here is the full information on the programs included:

1. Color Viewer
Browse through the Astrocade color palette eight colors at a time.
Features

  *   Displays eight consecutive colors per page.
  *   Joystick cycles pages.
  *   Knob allows fast color jumps with a trigger interlock.

2. Color Matcher
Compare and adjust multiple colors at once.
Features

  *   Four independent color rows.
  *   Select a row and adjust its color using the joystick.
  *   Knob allows fast cycling, also with trigger interlock.

3. Color Table (New)
Displays all 64 colors per page in a large grid with an independently adjustable background.
Features

  *   Displays full 64-color tables per page.
  *   Joystick left and right moves between pages. Pulling the trigger limits movement to a single column shift.
  *   Joystick up and down changes the background color.
  *   Knob provides fast background color cycling.
  *   Very helpful for choosing contrasting foreground and background colors on real hardware.

Enjoy!

The following is a work description informing one how to:
1. Alter the WOW ROM 1 file labeled wow.x1, which executes at the system reset location 0000H.
2. Load the altered wow.x1 file into the WOW 7 ROM set folder.
3. Open the MAME Debugger and run the altered Z80 coded program residing at 0000H.

This work description utilizes the Windows operating system and the HxD hex viewer/editor software.

INITIAL SET UP

The MAME Emulation folder contains the mame64.exe application folder along with a roms folder. The roms folder contains the wow.zip folder, which contains the 7 WOW ROM coding files.

Copy wow.zip and paste it to a desirable location. You could create a WOW Emulation or AstrocadeHR folder and paste wow.zip there. This copy will be your emergency access only "back up" wow.zip folder.

Open the wow.zip folder (that's in the roms folder) and copy the wow.x1 file.
Paste the copy into your Documents library.
This copy will be your wow.x1 "recovery" file (contains the original wow.x1 coding).
Paste a copy also into your Music library.
This copy will be your "altered" wow.x1 file.

USE HxD TO PRINT OUT THE ORIGINAL CODING WITHIN THE wow.x1 FILE

Open the HxD software.
Select "File", then "Open..." to open up the HxD navigation window.
Select the "Documents" library on the left and load the wow.x1 file there into HxD.
This file's Z80 coding should appear in the main HxD window.
Select "File", then "Print" to print out the original wow.x1 coding.

Use this printout as a visual reference showing you the original wow.x1 coding.
The printout may come in handy when you are altering the wow.x1 file coding.

The WOW ROMs are 4KB. A ROM printout will show the ROM's internal op coding from 0000 - 0FFFH.

ALTERING OP CODES IN THE wow.x1 FILE

Open the HxD software.
Select "File", then "Open..." to open up the HxD navigation window.

When you are altering code, pay attention to which wow.x1 file you are loading into HxD.
The wow.x1 in the Music library is the altering file.
The wow.x1 in the Documents library is the recovery (original coding) file.

Point to the file in the Music library to load the altering wow.x1 file into HxD.

You can use the mouse or left/right/up/down direction keys to point the HxD cursor to the desired opcode.

Use keys 0-9, A-F to enter new hex digits.
Any hex digit change will appear red in color.
An incorrect digit can be corrected by simply writing over it.

When you're finished altering codes, select "File", then "Save" to save your changes.
Note: You can confirm your alterations using the MAME Debugger program pane.

LOAD THE ALTERED wow.x1 FILE INTO THE WOW 7 ROM CODING FILES LISTING

Navigate to the altered wow.x1 file in the Music library.
Copy that file.

Now, navigate to the wow.zip file and open it.
You will see the 7 ROM files wow.x1 thru wow.x7 there.

Point to wow.x1 to delete it. When you select delete, a delete warning window will appear.
Note that this deletion will NOT be directed to the recycle bin.
Select "Delete" to delete the wow.x1 file.
Now, point inside the ROM listing window, then right-click and select "paste".
You will see the (altered) wow.x1 file appear on top of the 7 ROM files listing.
You're done, so close the ROM listing window.

OPEN THE MAME DEBUGGER

Left click the Windows start button (bottom left corner of screen).
Enter the abbreviated word  com  in the neighboring "text input area", then press the "Enter" key.
Com is a command to open the command prompt window.
The command prompt window will appear.
You will see a short navigation path (beginning with the C: drive) and ending with a blinking cursor.
You will have to extend this navigation path (NP) to point to the folder which contains the
mame64.exe application file, which is the MAME Emulation folder.
To enter the correct navigation path, navigate to the MAME Emulation folder, then open it.
At the top of this open window, you should see the navigation path (NP) that you need to add to the command prompt NP.

You CAN'T extend the NP in the command prompt directly using your keyboard.
You have to use an abbreviated  cd  command to extend this NP.
You CAN extend the command prompt NP using just 1 cd instruction.
For example, in my Windows 7 setup, I would enter at the blinking cursor,
cd Astrocade/Astrocade Emulation/MAME Emulation
then press the "Enter" key.
This cd command would add that new extension to the NP.
Note the "slashes" must tilt to the right as shown above, not to the left.

You're not done yet. You must also enter
mame64 wow -debug
or alternately
mame64 -debug wow
You don't need the cd command to add this entry. Just key it in.
The cursor should now be blinking at the very end of "debug" (or alternately "wow")
The label wow is the name of the emulation game you are loading into the MAME Debugger.
Note the game name wow matches wow.zip and wow.x1.

Now check your NP to confirm there are no errors, then press the "Enter" key.

If you entered the correct extended NP you should see a large black window with stars plus the Debug window.

TOUR THE OPENED MAME DEBUGGER

The black star field window is actually the game screen display.
At this point the game execution is in the "pause mode".

The debugger window has 3 panes.
Left pane
Lists the Z80 registers, the interrupt mode (IM), the Halt line and other info.
Top pane
Shows a portion of the program, listing the respective ROM addresses, Z80 mnemonics and Z80 opcodes.
Note that the program disassembled mneumonic instructions some times may be incorrect.
Bottom pane
Includes a message field and a debugger command entry area with a blinking cursor.

RUN A LOADED MAME GAME

If you don't alter wow.x1, you will be able to run the original WOW coin-op game on the debugger screen display.

Point/click Debug (upper left-hand corner of the Debug window), then point/click "Run" in the drop-down menu.

You can move the game screen display left and the Debug window right to see the entire screen display.

Point-and-click the screen display window, then press the key P to pause the game.
Press P again to resume gameplay.

Press F3 to emulate a system reset.
Press F2 to activate the WOW onboard self test.
Press F2 again to exit self test, which also executes a system reset.

If you close the Debug window, the screen display will remain.

If you close the screen display window first, you will also close the Debug window.

If you continually press the "right direction" key, you will be able to easily enter mame64 wow -debug again in the command prompt window NP. Nice option!

Confirm your coding alterations using the debugger program pane.
You can scroll that program down and up.
Note the program listing initiates at the system reset location 0000H.

You can open an error log window.

This window may display error messages during gameplay.
You can clear this window at any time. Click the window "Log", then click "Clear".

The command prompt window will display any checksum errors and the elapsed game/program run time in secs.

     "MICRO PAC is a colorful imitation of the coin-op PAC-MAN, with nice graphics and three levels of difficulty.  H.A.R.D. has done an excellent job of reproducing the PAC-MAN playfield in BASIC.  It even looks better than Atari 2600 PAC-MAN. Granted, difficulty level three is faster, but it's impossible to play, due to the ghosts' ability to go through the walls.
     The root of the problem with MICRO PAC is that apparently, there are no Machine Language routines in the actual game-play, although the graphics are created in Machine Language.  That is why it plays so slowly, and why only one character at a time can move on the screen.  In addition, no "clean-up" routines were programmed, with the result being that debris is left scattered throughout the playfield, such as half a ghost, etc.  This could be an excellent game, if it were programmed completely in Machine Language; but it's not, so it's mediocre, at best."

From the manual:

----------

The Ayatollah adds a new dimension to tic-tac-toe: cheating! His eyes and mouth move as he constantly changes his mind, changes his moves and changes the rules!  Can you beat him by playing fair? Can you exercise diplomatic restraint?  Will you take an axe to your computer? May Allah be with you!

PLAYING THE GAME

The game begins when the Ayatollah decides who starts.  He may change his mind.  The tic-tac-toe board is numbered 1 through 9, exactly like the keyboard, as follows:

7 8 9
4 5 6
1 2 3

To enter your move (human always plays X, but does not always start first), simply press the key of the square you wish to fill. That’s all there is to it. Well, sort of...

You see, the program is a heuristic algorithm.  That means it's a problem solving routine with a little bit of the human thought process thrown in.  It can be beaten.  Keep telling yourself that. It will play fairly as long as it needs to.  It can beat you without cheating if you make bad moves.  But if you get it into a situation where it can only lose on the next move, it will cheat.  You can still win if you can trick it into cheating its way into a trap.  We have also left it blind to one situation which we will leave it to you to discover.   We do want you to win.  We're on your side... really!  And we don't want you to get mad and smash your computer, because then you won’t buy any more of HARD's programs...

Oh, by the way: no "cat's games."  The Ayatollah takes all ties!

    "TIC TAC TOLLAH is, as you can probably guess, a Tic-Tac-Toe game and a pretty nice one.  The graphic display of the Ayatollah is excellent, even though it is not in color.
     In this version of Tic-Tac-Toe, you play against the computer.  But even if you win, you lose, 'cause that's the kinda guy the Ayatollah is, and that's what makes this particular Tic-Tac-Toe game interesting."

The Crown Of Zeus by Todd Johnson is a very unique RPG for AstroBASIC. And this made the rest of the Gibeleous series a major gap in our tape library. So, I very much appreciated when Allen Schweitzer picked up a complete Gibeleous series tape on eBay. In some ways, this is be careful what you wish for, because the first sequel, Rescue Of Catherine, has an extremely annoying gimmick. Almost all combat is deadly. If you find an enemy, it will kill you whether you fight or flee, and a magic amulet transports you back to the beginning of the maze. So, you have to find a path where you can sneak past the enemies. However, I persevered, and did finally manage to save Catherine (and confirm the dump is good). I'll attach a guide in case anyone else wants to complete this without pulling their hair out. Although honestly, there's not much to it if you don't explore on your own.

The basic gameplay is the same as The Crown Of Zeus from Arcadian volume 5, issue 1. The actions are 1 to fight, 2 to leave the room, and 3 to rest. If you select to leave the room, enter a letter for the direction to go (NESWUD). Eventually, you reach a room with no enemies and no exits. This means it's time to load the next set of levels. Press the HALT key, then enter:
R=R-24;:INPUT @(0),192 GO
Load the extra level data and you're ready to play again. Note that if you die at this point, you'll save to reset and reload from the very beginning.

At any point, you can HALT the program and use :PRINT to save your progress. Definitely save periodically if you want to finish this on your own.

Does anyone want to help test the other programs--The Crown of Zeus from the tape, Escape From Rantanam IV, and The Tower Of Machor?

It's too bad this didn't come with instructions, as there may have been additional story details in those.

I added the game "1024" by Tony Mokonen, a BASIC program written in 2023.  It is available in Bally BASIC, AstroBASIC and Blue Ram BASIC.

When the program was shared with the Astrocade discussion group, the author wrote "I do have a second game completed.  It's a version of 2048 (https://play2048.co/)."

You can read more about the "2048" videogame on its Wikipedia page, here:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2048_(video_game)

Tony continues, "I divided all the numbers by 2, because I didn't want to overflow the 16 bit variable I was using to keep score.  It's written very generically, using no graphics and the & array to generate sound, so that it will run in different versions of BASIC.  I did that because I wanted to use it as benchmark to test the speed of the various versions of BASIC on the Astrocade.  It's actually quite a noticeable speed difference between the original Bally BASIC and the versions that came later.  Blue Ram Basic is the winner as far as speed."

For those who like to know how a program functions, there is commented BASIC source code included in each archive.  Tony carefully wrote the program so that identical code runs for each version of the game.  As he says in his comments, the Blue Ram BASIC version plays fastest, while the AstroBASIC version comes in second place and the Bally BASIC version is quite slow.
